faq.a: Pass-through uses architecture or a body as the barrier. Through-object-in enters via a named prop such as a keyhole or cup, often with a scale change.

faq.q: When should I use Pass Through?
faq.a: Use it to change rooms without a cut, or to make a building feel like a mechanism. Do not use it as a cheap wipe.

faq.q: How do I prompt Pass Through for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the barrier and the arrival space, and keep the path continuous. Example: Pass-through of [Subject], the camera traveling through a wall, a body, a window as if matter were optional.

title: Pedestal Down
narrative: Return to human height after a high formal view, or sit the camera down to a child, a table, a wound. Because tilt is constant, the world does not bow; we simply stand lower in it.
It is the wrong tool when you must look down as you drop, or when the arm should swing over a railing. If pitch changes, you left the pedestal.
how: Translate on Y only. Keep tilt, and usually keep yaw.
Vertical parallax reverses the up-move: architecture climbs the frame. Prompt a pedestal down, camera lowering vertically, no tilt, a calm descent through the same axis.
when: Use it to return to human height after a high formal view. Concrete beat: from a chandelier's height down to the couple, still looking along the ballroom, not down at the floor.
Do not tilt to keep them in frame; change height instead.
vs: A Crane Down can arc, advance, and even hand off to a walk. A Tilt Down pitches from a fixed height.
Pedestal Up is the opposite column. Pedestal down sits the camera down while it keeps looking the same way.
examples_film: Barry Lyndon favors formal, measured height and locked geometry over swooping arms. 2001: A Space Odyssey again treats vertical station as a physical fact of the set.
Use them as tilt-locked descent grammar.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Tilt Down or Crane Down . The tell is a nodding horizon or a curved path over furniture.
The fix: straight drop, tilt frozen, end at the new eyeline.

faq.q: What is Pedestal Down in film?
faq.a: It is a straight vertical lowering of the camera with tilt unchanged, so the lens occupies a lower station without nodding.

faq.q: Pedestal Down vs Crane Down
faq.a: Crane down travels on an arm and often changes angle as it arrives. Pedestal down is a column drop: same pitch, new height.

faq.q: When should I use Pedestal Down?
faq.a: When rank or scale should change by sitting the camera down, not by looking down. Do not use it to dive at a face from a rooftop.

faq.q: How do I prompt Pedestal Down for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write camera lowers straight down on a pedestal, tilt constant, no arc. Name the start height and the settle.

title: Pedestal Up
narrative: Height changes without the drama of a crane arc. You are still looking the same way, only from higher, so rank and horizon shift together.
It is a formal lift, useful when the camera must stay architecturally true. It is the wrong tool when you need to boom out over a crowd or ease back as you rise.
A pedestal does not draw an arc; a crane does.
how: Use a studio pedestal, a column, or a virtual Y-axis translate. Lock tilt and usually lock yaw.

The nodal point gains height, so you get vertical parallax: near objects drop faster than the far skyline. Prompt a pedestal up, camera rising vertically on a column with no tilt change, eyeline climbing.
when: Use it to change height without the drama of a crane arc. Concrete beat: from a tabletop to the standing speaker, looking the same direction the whole way.
Do not add a tilt-up and call it a pedestal.
vs: A Crane Up arcs through space and often eases backward, changing X and Z as well as Y. A Tilt Up only pitches from a fixed height.
A Jib Shot is a short pivoting arm, so its path is an arc, not a column. Pedestal Down is the same column the other way.
examples_film: 2001: A Space Odyssey treats vertical camera placement as spacecraft geometry rather than as a flourish. Studio multi-camera drama uses the pedestal column as the default lift.
Pair those as grammar for tilt-locked height, not as a look to clone.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Tilt Up or a Crane Up . The tell is a pitching horizon, or a backward boom that reveals a city.
The fix: straight Y travel, tilt locked, no arc.

faq.q: What is Pedestal Up in film?
faq.a: It is a straight vertical rise of the whole camera with tilt held constant, so you look from a higher station in the same direction.

faq.q: Pedestal Up vs Crane Up
faq.a: Crane up follows an arm's arc and often backs away. Pedestal up is a column: height only, pitch unchanged.

faq.q: When should I use Pedestal Up?
faq.a: When you need a clean height change and a stable horizon, often in architecture or studio blocking. Do not use it for a skyline reveal that requires boom-out.

faq.q: How do I prompt Pedestal Up for AI image or video?
faq.a: Say camera rises straight up on a pedestal, no tilt change, no crane arc. Name start height and end height.

title: Pull Out
narrative: Show the container around a feeling. The person remains while the world claims them.

Unlike a zoom out, furniture and doorways can pass the lens because the camera is retreating. It is the wrong tool when you needed a high aerial to let land win, and the wrong tool when a locked optical widen would be more detached.
Define whose viewpoint the retreat represents.
how: Translate backward on dolly, Steadicam, or virtual camera. Fix focal length.
Compose the wide end so the new walls mean something. Prompt a slow pull out, intimacy widening into environment, the person remaining while the world claims them.
when: Use it to show the container around a feeling. Concrete beat: a crying close coverage that retreats until the empty apartment is the sentence.
Do not pull out into a blank sky with no new fact.
vs: A Dolly Out is this job on wheels at human height. An Aerial Pullback leaves the ground.
A Slow Zoom Out discloses context without walking. Pull out is the generic physical or virtual retreat: the container appears because we backed up.
examples_film: The Truman Show discloses the constructed world by leaving the intimate frame. The Player uses retreat as part of longer moving sentences that reveal the lot as a system.
Treat them as container grammar, not as setups to duplicate.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Slow Zoom Out . The tell is no parallax as the room grows.
The fix: move the camera away, fixed lens, new architecture passing the edges.

faq.q: What is Pull Out in film?
faq.a: It is a camera retreat that opens space around a subject because the station point moves away, not because the lens widens alone.

faq.q: Pull Out vs Dolly Out
faq.a: Dolly out names the wheeled path. Pull out is the broader retreat job and may be Steadicam, virtual, or track. Both should show parallax; a zoom out will not.

faq.q: When should I use Pull Out?
faq.a: When the room, street, or system around a feeling is the next sentence. Do not use it as an aerial chapter-close.

faq.q: How do I prompt Pull Out for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write slow pull out, camera moving away, environment entering, no optical zoom. Name the container that must appear.

title: Push In
narrative: A thought lands. Do not rush it.
The job is the realization, the lie, the trap, not the display of a rig. Parallax still appears, even if the travel is only a meter, because the station point changes.

It is the wrong tool when you wanted optical compression from a locked body, and the wrong tool when you wanted a long track into a room as geography. If you add a second flourish, the thought is gone.
how: Dolly, slider, Steadicam, or virtual camera on the Z axis, usually from medium to medium close-up. Keep the lens fixed so the push is distance, not zoom.
Tiny parallax is the honesty. Prompt an imperceptibly slow push in, medium into medium close-up, walls closing before the motion is noticed.
when: Use it when a thought lands and you should not rush it. Concrete beat: a listener understands they are caught, medium to MCU over 6 seconds.
Do not push in on every line.
vs: A Dolly In names the wheeled support and often travels farther, as geography. A Slow Zoom In never moves the camera, so there is no parallax.
Push in is the pressure beat: short, physical or virtual, tied to a thought. If the track is a room long, you are dollying.
examples_film: The Silence of the Lambs uses slow physical approaches so conversations become traps. The Shining and There Will Be Blood let small advances register as mental weather.
Use the patience and the parallax, not a particular actor's blocking as a clone.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Slow Zoom In . The tell is enlargement without sliding foreground.
The fix: translate closer, fixed lens, short path, end on the thought, no extra move.

faq.q: What is Push In in film?
faq.a: It is a short, usually slow advance of the camera toward a subject so the frame tightens because the lens occupies a nearer station.

faq.q: Push In vs Dolly In
faq.a: Dolly in specifies a wheeled or tracked translation and can be a long geographic enter. Push in is the pressure job: often shorter, sometimes virtual, always tied to a thought landing.

faq.q: When should I use Push In?
faq.a: When a realization or trap should close the air around a face. Do not use it as a default on every close-up.

faq.q: How do I prompt Push In for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write very slow push in, camera walking closer, medium to MCU, 6 seconds, no optical zoom. Mention slight parallax.

title: Rapid Zoom In
narrative: No time for a dolly. Emphasis as a weapon: a face, a gun, a sign.
The snap is so short it can read as an axial cut with a trail of glass. A crash zoom is already fast; this is faster than a polite crash.
If you can feel a leisurely enlarge, it is not rapid. If the body moved, you dollied.
how: Locked sticks or a locked handheld brace, zoom thrown to the end stop in a fraction of a second, then hold. Wide to tight.
No parallax. Prompt: Rapid zoom in on [Subject], faster than a polite crash, almost a cut, the world snapping tight.
when: Use it when a fact must arrive as a snap, not a walk. Do not use it on every line.
vs: Crash Zoom In is the punch that is still readable as a zoom. Rapid is nearer a cut.
YoYo Zoom comes back out. A true cut would have no optical trail.
examples_film: Hot Fuzz weaponizes snap zooms as punctuation. Kill Bill uses snap zooms as comic and violent emphasis.
Grammar: almost a cut, then a hold.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a dolly-in or a slow crash. The tell: parallax, or a leisurely enlarge.
The fix: locked body, snap to tight in a few frames, hold.

faq.q: What is Rapid Zoom In in film?
faq.a: A rapid zoom in is an extremely fast optical snap into the subject, almost a cut, then a hold. The camera body stays put.

faq.q: Rapid Zoom In vs Crash Zoom In
faq.a: A crash zoom in is a fast but readable punch. Rapid zoom in is faster than a polite crash, nearer to a cut with a trail of glass.

faq.q: When should I use Rapid Zoom In?
faq.a: Use it when there is no time for a dolly and the fact must snap tight. Do not use it on every line.

faq.q: How do I prompt Rapid Zoom In for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write an extremely fast zoom, then a hold. Example: Rapid zoom in on [Subject], faster than a polite crash, almost a cut, the world snapping tight.

title: Rapid Zoom Out
narrative: Reveal as a joke or a shock. A close face becomes a tiny figure in a huge problem: a crowd, a desert, a mess.
The snap is the gag. A pull-out walks away with parallax.
A crash zoom out is the readable cousin. Rapid is the snap.
If the environment does not suddenly exist, you only loosened a portrait.
how: Locked body, zoom thrown wide in a few frames, then hold. Tight to wide.
Prompt: Rapid zoom out from [Subject], the environment exploding into view in a snap.
when: Use it to reveal scale or context as a shock. Do not use a slow zoom out and call it rapid.
vs: Crash Zoom Out is the readable optical reverse. Pull Out translates the camera away.
Rapid zoom out is the snap to a wide, then a hold, body still.
examples_film: Shaun of the Dead snaps out to dump a person into a problem. Scott Pilgrim uses snap outs as graphic punctuation.
Grammar: environment exploding into view.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a pull-out. The tell: the camera walked, lamps sheared.
The fix: lock the body, snap the glass wide, hold on the new map.

faq.q: What is Rapid Zoom Out in film?
faq.a: A rapid zoom out is a snap from the subject to a wide in a few frames, environment exploding into view, then a hold. No body travel.

faq.q: Rapid Zoom Out vs Pull Out
faq.a: A pull-out physically retreats and produces parallax. Rapid zoom out only changes focal length, as a snap, then holds.

faq.q: When should I use Rapid Zoom Out?
faq.a: Use it to reveal context as a shock or a joke. Do not use it as a slow opener.

faq.q: How do I prompt Rapid Zoom Out for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write a snap to a wide, then a hold. Example: Rapid zoom out from [Subject], the environment exploding into view in a snap.

title: Road Rush
narrative: Intros to chases, night highways, a nightmare of driving: get down and let tarmac fill the frame. Lane dashes streak; light becomes paint.
A standing-height car commercial is not this shot. FPV is flight; this is tarmac.
Do not rise to a pretty three-quarter beauty pass unless you end there on purpose.
how: Low mount, bumper height or below, wide, shutter that allows streak. Lane lines, cat's eyes, wet asphalt.
Motion blur as paint. Prompt: Road-rush of [Subject], low to the asphalt, speed as smear, headlights and lane lines as weapons.
when: Use it when the road is the event. Do not use it as a default car portrait from chest height.
vs: Car Chasing keeps two machines in a hunt. FPV Drone leaves the ground.
Motion Blur is a shutter fact that road-rush uses as grammar. Road-rush can exist with no car in frame at all.
examples_film: Tron Legacy's highway treats lanes as weapons of light. Death Proof keeps the camera down on asphalt as a threat.
Grammar: low, fast, tarmac as the subject.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a car commercial from standing height. The tell: you can read the whole vehicle cleanly and the asphalt is a thin strip.
The fix: drop to the tarmac, streak the lanes, let the road own the frame.

faq.q: What is Road Rush in film?
faq.a: Road rush is a low camera on asphalt at speed, with lane lines and headlights streaking. The road is the subject.

faq.q: Road Rush vs Car Chasing
faq.a: Car chasing covers pursuit from a second vehicle. Road rush can ignore the hunter and treat tarmac, lanes, and smear as the event.

faq.q: When should I use Road Rush?
faq.a: Use it for night highways, chase intros, and driving as threat. Do not use it as a standing-height product pass.

faq.q: How do I prompt Road Rush for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write a low rush along asphalt with streaking lanes. Example: Road-rush of [Subject], low to the asphalt, speed as smear, headlights and lane lines as weapons.

title: Robo Arm
narrative: The path must be identical every take. Commercials, previs stages , a bottle that must match a CGI pass, a stunt that must fit a plate: the arm does not interpret.
A human dolly will drift. An orbit-360 can be walked and will breathe.
Bolt cam is a throw, not a repeatable spline (unless the throw is itself robotic). If you want error and life, do not use the arm.
how: Motion-control arm or a six-axis robot, programmed XYZ and pan/tilt/roll. Speed can be inhumanly even or inhumanly fast.
Product tables, crash pads, or a repeatable orbit. Prompt: Robotic arm move around [Subject], programmed path, inhuman precision, product or stunt geometry.
when: Use it when takes must match: VFX, product, a stunt plate. Do not use it for a scene that needs human drift.
vs: 360-Degree Orbit can be a human walk or a circular dolly with breath. Bolt Cam is a crash throw aimed at impact.
Robo-arm is the repeatable spline, any shape, no shake.
examples_film: Commercials and previs stages are the native grammar: bottles, cars, and stunt geometry that must composite. The precision is the style.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a steadicam orbit. The tell: a little sway, a human accel.
The fix: write programmed path, identical takes, no operator shake.

faq.q: What is Robo Arm in film?
faq.a: A robo arm is a robotic camera on a programmed path, repeatable every take, with no human shake. Product and stunt geometry live here.

faq.q: Robo Arm vs 360-Degree Orbit
faq.a: An orbit-360 is a circular walk or dolly and can breathe. A robo arm can orbit, but the point is a programmed spline that matches take to take.

faq.q: When should I use Robo Arm?
faq.a: Use it when the path must be identical: VFX plates, product, stunts. Do not use it when you want human error.

faq.q: How do I prompt Robo Arm for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write a programmed path with no shake. Example: Robotic arm move around [Subject], programmed path, inhuman precision, product or stunt geometry.

title: Slider Shot
narrative: A full dolly is too much. A few centimeters of travel can prove the room has depth: a microphone in the foreground slides against a face, a bottle turns against a window.
The move is small on purpose. It is the wrong tool for a city block, and the wrong tool if you needed a curve around a product.
If the rail is meters long, you are dollying. If the path is a circle, you are orbiting.
how: Clamp a short rail, level it, choose a constant speed. Keep the move lateral or a tiny push; do not hide a zoom inside it.
Prompt a short slider move, 60 to 120 centimeters of lateral travel, product or interview parallax, precise and small.
when: Use it when a full dolly is too much and a lock-off needs a little parallax. Concrete beat: an interview single with a lamp sliding in the foreground over 6 seconds.
Do not slider a chase.
vs: A Dolly Left is the same linear idea at room or street scale. An 360-Degree Orbit is curved and long.
A Push In may use a slider as the rail, but push in is the Z-axis thought; slider names the short linear tool. Slider is compact travel, not a path through architecture.
examples_film: The grammar is commercial and interview more than a single famous scene: tabletop product films , documentary talking heads, small table moves inside features. Use the 60-to-120-centimeter parallax, not a particular ad to clone.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a full Dolly Left or a tiny 360-Degree Orbit . The tell is meters of travel, or a curve.
The fix: name the short rail, linear path, subtle parallax, end still in the same room.

faq.q: What is Slider Shot in film?
faq.a: It is a short linear camera move on a compact rail, typically under about 120 centimeters, used to add small parallax to a still setup.

faq.q: Slider Shot vs Dolly Left
faq.a: Dolly left can travel a room or a street. A slider is the compact rail version: interview, product, a lamp sliding against a face.

faq.q: When should I use Slider Shot?
faq.a: When a lock-off feels dead and a full track would be too much. Do not use it as a substitute for covering a walk.

faq.q: How do I prompt Slider Shot for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write short slider, 60 to 120 centimeters, lateral, subtle parallax, 6 seconds. Ban a long dolly and ban a circular orbit.

title: Slow Zoom In
narrative: The shot is a thought that closes without walking. Geography stays put, so the audience feels watched or analyzed rather than approached.
Faces grow, walls stay in the same relation, and the pressure is optical. Use it when attention must narrow and the room must not rearrange itself.
It is the wrong tool when you need to enter a mind by occupying the same air: that job belongs to a physical approach, because a zoom never changes the camera's station point.
how: Lock a heavy tripod. Keep height, tilt, and nodal point still.
Drive focal length smoothly over several seconds and rehearse focus compensation as depth of field shallows. Compression increases: distant planes look closer to the subject even though nobody moved.
Prompt a locked camera body, a gradual optical zoom in, rising compression, and an explicit ban on dolly parallax.
when: Use it to raise pressure on a still figure while the architecture stays legally the same. Concrete beat: a surveillance long-lens slowly isolating one person in a crowd.
Do not use it if foreground objects must peel and prove the camera walked.
vs: A Dolly In translates the whole camera, so foreground and background change speed. A Push In is a physical or virtual walk whose job is a realization landing.
A Crash Zoom In uses the same optical mechanism at sting speed. Stay on slow zoom in when the station point must not move.
examples_film: The Conversation isolates figures in Union Square with a gradual long-lens close. There Will Be Blood and Phantom Thread use slow optical tightening as patience and scrutiny.
These are grammar for locked-body compression, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Dolly In or a digital crop sold as a zoom. The tell is parallax: if a foreground chair slides against the wall, you translated.
The fix is a locked head, a true focal-length change, and a hold on the final tight frame.

faq.q: What is Slow Zoom In in film?
faq.a: It is a gradual increase of focal length with the camera support still. The image tightens and space compresses, but the camera does not occupy a new position.

faq.q: Slow Zoom In vs Dolly In
faq.a: Dolly in walks the camera so perspective and parallax change. Slow zoom in only walks the lens: size grows, relative geometry of planes stays the same.

faq.q: When should I use Slow Zoom In?
faq.a: When you want pressure, scrutiny, or a slow isolation and you need the room to remain the same place. Skip it if the beat is actually entering the space.

faq.q: How do I prompt Slow Zoom In for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name a locked tripod, optical zoom in, duration, and no body travel. Example: camera body locked, lens slowly zooming in for 6 seconds, compression increasing, no dolly.

title: Slow Zoom Out
narrative: The joke, the trap, or the social system was already around the person. The lens simply admits it.

Because the station point is unchanged, the reveal feels observational: we were always this far away, we only chose to see more. It is the wrong tool when the camera must retreat through a doorway, lose a foreground, or leave someone behind in real space.
Optical widening cannot walk out of a room.
how: Lock the tripod and reverse the zoom. Start on a composed tight frame and pre-compose the wide end so heads, signs, and negative space land.
Focus will deepen as focal length shortens. Prompt a tripod-locked optical zoom out, no camera body travel, and name what architecture must appear by the last frame.
when: Use it to reveal context, isolation, or an off-screen joke that was already in the location. Concrete beat: a tight face opening onto a dinner table that has been watching.
Do not use it to exit a location: that is a physical pull.
vs: A Pull Out and a Dolly Out move the camera backward, so foreground objects leave the frame with parallax. A slow zoom out only changes the lens angle of view.
If you also need a Slow Zoom In cousin in the same scene, keep both bodies locked so the pair stays optical.
examples_film: Barry Lyndon widens into painterly social tableaux without walking the camera into the party. The Social Network , Her, and Lost in Translation use slow optical opening to place a person inside a system they cannot leave.
Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Dolly Out . The tell is a sliding foreground: plants, shoulders, or door jambs changing their overlap.
The fix is to freeze the support and drive only focal length, then hold the wide.

faq.q: What is Slow Zoom Out in film?
faq.a: It is a gradual decrease of focal length from a locked camera, so the frame widens while the camera's position stays the same.

faq.q: Slow Zoom Out vs Dolly Out
faq.a: Dolly out retreats through space and creates parallax. Slow zoom out stays on the sticks and only widens the lens, so planes keep their original perspective relation.

faq.q: When should I use Slow Zoom Out?
faq.a: When the surrounding situation is the punchline or the prison, and you want to disclose it without relocating the camera. Do not use it as a substitute for leaving the room.

faq.q: How do I prompt Slow Zoom Out for AI image or video?
faq.a: State locked tripod, optical zoom out, and what must be revealed. Example: tripod locked, lens slowly zooming out for 6 seconds, architecture entering, no body travel.

title: SnorriCam
narrative: Trap the audience in a body that cannot get out. Panic, intoxication, or dissociation becomes spatial because the person is locked to the image and the street will not sit still.
It is the wrong tool for a first-person view of what they see. A SnorriCam faces the wearer.
It is not a body-cam showing the world, and it is not a follow from behind.
how: Use a safely fitted lightweight body rig, or reproduce the relative motion in a virtual scene. Preserve tiny bodily movements without letting the face float independently of the torso.
Prompt a SnorriCam body-mounted on the subject, camera locked to the torso, face pinned, world sloshing behind.
when: Use it to trap the audience in a body that cannot get out. Concrete beat: a panicked walk down a sidewalk, pupils steady in frame, storefronts shearing.
Do not use it as POV of the sidewalk.
vs: Point of View shows what they look at, from beside or as them. Handheld is an operator nearby, not bolted to the chest.
Locked-On glues the camera to a subject that may not be the wearer, often from outside a vehicle or a fall. SnorriCam is body-mounted and facing the actor.
examples_film: Requiem for a Dream uses body-mounted shots during panic and disorientation. Pi destabilizes Max's movement through the city with a pinned face.
Mean Streets is part of the same body-rig family. Face stable, world not: that is the grammar.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Point of View or a Follow Shot from behind. The tell is seeing the street as the actor would, or seeing their back.
The fix: camera on the body, pointed at the face, background shearing.

faq.q: What is SnorriCam in film?
faq.a: It is a camera rigged to the performer and aimed at them, so their face stays oddly stable while the environment moves around it.

faq.q: SnorriCam vs Point of View
faq.a: POV shows what the person sees. SnorriCam shows the person, locked to their torso, with the world unmoored behind them.

faq.q: When should I use SnorriCam?
faq.a: When panic, drugs, or dissociation should trap us in a body. Do not use it as a helmet-cam of the street.

faq.q: How do I prompt SnorriCam for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write body-mounted camera locked to the torso, face centered and pinned, background sliding wildly. Ban POV of the environment.

title: Static Locked-Off
narrative: Trust blocking and duration. Movement would be noise.

Comedy, ritual, and dread all live here because the audience cannot be rescued by a pan when something enters, or fails to enter, the rectangle. It is the wrong tool when geography must be discovered in motion, and the wrong tool if you add a slider 'for life' and destroy the contract.
Silence of the head is a relationship to the action, not a frozen audio file.
how: Heavy sticks, locked head, level bubble, no touch after slate. Actors and air may move; the camera may not.
Prompt a perfectly static locked-off shot, heavy tripod, zero camera movement, composition doing all the work.
when: Use it when blocking and duration should carry the beat and movement would be noise. Concrete beat: a domestic task held in a fixed composition until the task changes meaning.
Do not drift.
vs: A Tableau is a related still, often more presentational. A Long Take may be static or moving; length is not the lock-off.
Any dolly, pan, or zoom leaves this family. Static is zero camera path.
examples_film: Jeanne Dielman holds domestic tasks in fixed compositions. Tokyo Story lets rooms and sitting do the motion.
The Grand Budapest Hotel uses lock-offs as diagram. 2001: A Space Odyssey plants some spacecraft views as still geometry.
Grammar of the rectangle, not a kitchen to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a tiny Slider Shot or a breathing Handheld . The tell is any parallax or micro-pan.
The fix: locked head, no virtual drift, action inside a still frame.

faq.q: What is Static Locked-Off in film?
faq.a: It is a shot with no camera movement: the support is locked and only the world or the actors may move inside the composition.

faq.q: Static Locked-Off vs Long Take
faq.a: A long take is about duration and may travel. A static lock-off is about a frozen camera, whether the shot is 3 seconds or 3 minutes.

faq.q: When should I use Static Locked-Off?
faq.a: When blocking, comedy, or dread should happen inside a decided rectangle. Do not slide 'to add life' if the contract is stillness.

faq.q: How do I prompt Static Locked-Off for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write completely locked-off camera, heavy tripod, zero camera movement. Subject may breathe. Ban pan, dolly, zoom, and drift.

title: Steadicam
narrative: Long connecting moves through architecture. Light temperatures shift as rooms change.

The operator is walking, so the camera can turn corners, climb stairs, and arrive in a new social weather without laying track through every door. It is the wrong tool when you want documentary shake, or when a straight corridor would be cleaner and cheaper on track.
It is also not a gimbal: the isolation comes from a mechanical arm and the operator's trained gait, not from motors alone.
how: Vest, spring arm, sled, and a balanced camera. The operator walks a rehearsed line; the camera is isolated from footfall.
You can still boom slightly with the arm. Prompt Steadicam floating with the subject through connected spaces, preternatural smoothness, operator walking, no footfall shake.
when: Use it for long connecting moves through architecture, neither handheld nor dolly. Concrete beat: through a kitchen, down a stair, into a club, one path.
Do not Steadicam a lock-off that only needed sticks.
vs: A Gimbal Shot uses motorized electronic stabilization and is often run without a vest. Handheld keeps the operator's mass in the image as micro-tremor.
Tracking Shot is the job; Steadicam is a support that can execute tracks, follows, and Walk and Talk coverage. A Oner may be shot on Steadicam, but length of take is not the stabilizer.
examples_film: The Shining 's corridor work is the textbook Steadicam walk. Goodfellas ' Copa is a vest-and-arm descent through service spaces into a table.
Boogie Nights connects rooms as social circuits. Smooth path, human scale: that is the grammar.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Handheld shake added as a preset, or a Gimbal Shot clip that never feels like a vest. The tell is tremor, or a weightless electronic drift with no human gait.
The fix: name Steadicam, operator walking, isolated footfall, connected architecture.

faq.q: What is Steadicam in film?
faq.a: It is a mechanical stabilizer worn by an operator (vest, arm, sled) that lets the camera walk smoothly through spaces that track cannot easily enter.

faq.q: Steadicam vs Gimbal Shot
faq.a: Gimbal stabilization is motorized and often handheld without a vest. Steadicam isolates movement mechanically through an arm and trained operator gait.

faq.q: When should I use Steadicam?
faq.a: When you need a long, smooth walk through doorways and rooms. Do not use it as a synonym for any moving shot.

faq.q: How do I prompt Steadicam for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Steadicam, operator walking, floating smoothness, no footfall shake, through connected rooms. Name the path and the end room.

title: Super Dolly In
narrative: A normal dolly is not enough. The room is consumed: lamps, furniture, and walls shear hard, and the face is suddenly too close.
Threat, obsession, a corridor that becomes a portrait. A crash zoom does this optically with no shear.
A polite dolly-in keeps manners. Super is length plus speed plus violent parallax.
If the path is short, you only had a push.
how: Long track or a long steadicam drive on the lens axis, often wide at the start so the room can be eaten. Speed is high; the end is a close-up.
Prompt: Super dolly in on [Subject], a long aggressive travel that eats the room, parallax violent, the face arriving too fast.
when: Use it when approach must feel too much: a threat, a corridor, a face that arrives early. Do not use it for a gentle thought.
vs: Dolly In is the polite wheel-in, same axis, human speed. Crash Zoom In snaps glass from a locked body.
Super-dolly-in translates far and fast until the room is gone.
examples_film: The Shining 's long hotel approaches eat space toward a person, whether on wheels or a vest. Oldboy 's corridor drive-in is the grammar of a long aggressive travel that becomes a fight and a face.
Use them as space-eating approach, not as frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a crash zoom or a short push. The tell: no long shear of the room, or the whole picture simply enlarges.
The fix: a long physical path, violent parallax, face arriving too fast.

faq.q: What is Super Dolly In in film?
faq.a: A super dolly in is a long, fast physical approach that eats the room with violent parallax until the face is suddenly close.

faq.q: Super Dolly In vs Dolly In
faq.a: A dolly in is a controlled approach. Super dolly in is the same axis stretched in length and speed until geography collapses into a close-up.

faq.q: When should I use Super Dolly In?
faq.a: Use it when a polite approach is not enough: threat, corridor, obsession. Do not use it for a gentle thought.

faq.q: How do I prompt Super Dolly In for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write a long fast travel with violent parallax. Example: Super dolly in on [Subject], a long aggressive travel that eats the room, the face arriving too fast.

title: Super Dolly Out
narrative: Leave them in the system. A constructed world revealed, a street that was a room, a face that becomes a statistic of space.
The retreat is long enough that the map wins. An aerial pullback continues until land is everything.
Super-dolly-out stays on a human axis, wheels or vest, but the path is long and the dump is fast. A short pull-out only gives headroom.
how: Long reverse track on the lens axis, often starting close. Speed is high; end wide.
Parallax opens the room rather than eating it. Prompt: Super dolly out from [Subject], a long retreat that dumps the person into geography, the room exploding open.
when: Use it to dump a person into a larger system in one retreat. Do not use a short pull for headroom and call it super.
vs: Dolly Out is the polite reverse. Aerial Pullback leaves the human axis and wins as a map from the air.
Super-dolly-out stays grounded but goes far and fast.
examples_film: The Truman Show retreats until a constructed world owns the person. A reverse of the Copacabana energy (leaving the club instead of entering) is the grammar of dumping a figure back into a system.
Use them as long retreats, not as frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a zoom out or a short pull. The tell: the face shrinks with no shear, or the path is only a step.
The fix: long physical reverse, room exploding open, environment owning the frame.

faq.q: What is Super Dolly Out in film?
faq.a: A super dolly out is a long, fast physical retreat that dumps a person into geography until the environment owns the frame.

faq.q: Super Dolly Out vs Aerial Pullback
faq.a: An aerial pullback leaves by air until land is the subject. Super dolly out stays on a grounded axis but the reverse is long and the dump is fast.

faq.q: When should I use Super Dolly Out?
faq.a: Use it to leave someone inside a system that suddenly looks huge. Do not use a short pull for headroom.

faq.q: How do I prompt Super Dolly Out for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write a long reverse until the environment owns the frame. Example: Super dolly out from [Subject], a long retreat that dumps the person into geography.

title: Through Object In
narrative: Enter through a thing. Impossible reveals, jokes, a house tour that ignores walls: the named object is the door, not a generic wall.
Objects must keep thickness and shape during the passage. A cut from a cup to a face is not this.
Flying-cam transition punches architecture; this punches a prop. The practical task is continuity of space.
how: Build a 3D route and connect plates to digital interiors. Choose believable lens behavior and speed changes.
Name the object, the travel through it, and the arrival. Prompt: Through-object-in on [Subject], the camera entering via a cup, keyhole, speaker, or mouth, matter as a door.
when: Use it for an impossible reveal through a named object. Do not use a straight cut and call it a pass.
vs: Pass Through uses walls or bodies. Object Portal is the object-as-door idea.
Through Object Out is the reverse exit. Through-object-in arrives on the subject after the prop.
examples_film: Panic Room explores a townhouse through physically inaccessible openings. Fight Club opens from microscopic neural imagery into the narrator's predicament.
The Secret in Their Eyes passes from aerial into a crowd as if continuous. Being John Malkovich treats a portal as a door in a thing.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a cut from a cup to a face. The tell: no interior of the object, no thickness.
The fix: travel through the named prop, keep its shape, arrive on the far side.

faq.q: What is Through Object In in film?
faq.a: Through object in is a continuous camera path that enters via a named object (keyhole, cup, speaker, mouth) and arrives on the subject, often changing scale.

faq.q: Through Object In vs Pass Through
faq.a: Pass-through uses architecture or a body. Through-object-in uses a named prop as the door and often includes a scale change.

faq.q: When should I use Through Object In?
faq.a: Use it to enter a scene through a thing: a joke, an impossible house tour, a portal. Do not fake it with a cut.

faq.q: How do I prompt Through Object In for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the object, the travel, and the arrival. Example: Through-object-in on [Subject], the camera entering via a cup, keyhole, speaker, or mouth, matter as a door.

title: Through Object Out
narrative: Leave through a thing. Endings, a mind opening onto a city, a room that becomes a street by way of a window, a pupil, a barred frame: absence can be the dramatic center.
The effect is the viewpoint abandoning the person, not merely passing an obstacle. A zoom out that never enters matter is not this shot.
The object must occupy the frame as a tunnel.
how: Stage room, object, and exterior as one spatial problem. Removable barrier, support transfer, or composite.

Choreograph exterior action and offscreen sound to carry the event if the camera looks away. Prompt: Through-object-out from [Subject], the camera exiting via an object into a wider world, the interior becoming exterior.
when: Use it to leave a person through a thing into a larger space. Do not use a plain pull-out and claim a portal.
vs: Through Object In arrives. Aerial Pullback leaves by gaining altitude until geography wins, without needing a prop as tunnel.
Through-object-out needs the object as the exit.
examples_film: The Passenger 's late hotel-room shot moves toward and beyond a barred window, then looks back. Contact and The Tree of Life use exits of scale and matter as revelation.
Grammar: leave through a thing, interior becoming exterior.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a zoom out or a crane-up. The tell: the world enlarges but no object ever fills the frame as a passage.
The fix: occupy the lens with the object, travel through it, then the wider world.

faq.q: What is Through Object Out in film?
faq.a: Through object out is a moving viewpoint that leaves a subject by traveling out through an object into a larger space, interior becoming exterior.

faq.q: Through Object Out vs Through Object In
faq.a: Through-object-in enters via a prop and arrives on the person. Through-object-out exits via a prop and can abandon the person to a wider world.

faq.q: When should I use Through Object Out?
faq.a: Use it for endings and scale reveals that leave through a thing. Do not use a plain pull-out with no portal.

faq.q: How do I prompt Through Object Out for AI image or video?
faq.a: Start on the subject, travel out through a named object, arrive in a larger space. Example: Through-object-out from [Subject], the camera exiting via an object into a wider world.
